function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: This function generates a Dockerfile in the specified directory with basic configuration. The Dockerfile will be tailored to a simple Python application. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

expose_port.description: The port number that the container should expose. This is typically the port that the application listens on.

entrypoint.description: The command that will be executed when the Docker container starts.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

message.content:
Below is a **complete set of files** you can drop into the `nodejs-welcome` repository so that it can be containerised, deployed to Kubernetes, and built automatically on every push to `main`.  
I’ve written the files in a way that works with the typical structure of a minimal Node.js app (e.g. `app.js`, `package.json`, etc.). If your repo differs slightly, just adjust the paths or ports accordingly.

---

## 1. Dockerfile

```dockerfile
# Use the official Node.js 18 slim image as the base
FROM node:18-slim

# Set the working directory inside the container
WORKDIR /usr/src/app

# Copy package.json and package-lock.json first to leverage Docker cache
COPY package*.json ./

# Install production dependencies only
RUN npm ci --only=production

# Copy the rest of the application code
COPY . .

# Expose the port that the app listens on (default 3000)
EXPOSE 3000

# Start the application
CMD ["node", "app.js"]
```

> **Why this Dockerfile?**  
> * `node:18-slim` is small, stable, and contains everything you need to run a Node.js app.  
> * Installing dependencies before copying the source code lets Docker cache the `npm ci` layer, speeding up rebuilds.  
> * The container listens on port **3000** – change the `EXPOSE` line if your app uses a different port.

---

## 2. Kubernetes YAMLs

Create a single file `k8s/deployment.yaml` (you can keep it in a `k8s/` folder or at the repo root).  
It contains both the Deployment and Service definitions.

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome
  labels:
    app: nodejs-welcome
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome
        image: ghcr.io/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest   # <-- replace with your registry & tag
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
        env:
        - name: NODE_ENV
          value: production
        resources:
          limits:
            memory: "256Mi"
            cpu: "250m"
          requests:
            memory: "128Mi"
            cpu: "125m"

---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 80          # Service port
    targetPort: 3000  # Container port
```

> **Notes**  
> * Replace `ghcr.io/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest` with the actual image name/tag you’ll push to.  
> * The Service is `ClusterIP` by default; change `type:` to `NodePort` or `LoadBalancer` if you need external access.  
> * Adjust resource limits/requests to match your workload.

---

## 3. GitHub Actions Workflow

Create a file at `.github/workflows/ci.yml`:

```yaml
name: CI

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main

jobs:
  build-and-push:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
    - name: Checkout repository
      uses: actions/checkout@v4

    - name: Set up Docker Buildx
      uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v3

    - name: Log in to GitHub Container Registry
      uses: docker/login-action@v3
      with:
        registry: ghcr.io
        username: ${{ github.actor }}
        password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}

    - name: Build and push Docker image
      uses: docker/build-push-action@v5
      with:
        context: .
        file: Dockerfile
        push: true
        tags: ghcr.io/${{ github.repository }}:latest

    - name: Deploy to Kubernetes (optional)
      # Uncomment and configure if you have a cluster set up
      # uses: azure/k8s-deploy@v3
      # with:
      #   manifests: k8s/deployment.yaml
      #   kubeconfig: ${{ secrets.KUBE_CONFIG_DATA }}
```

> **What this workflow does**  
> 1. Triggers on every push to `main`.  
> 2. Builds the Docker image using the Dockerfile in the repo.  
> 3. Pushes the image to GitHub Container Registry (`ghcr.io`).  
> 4. (Optional) Deploys to a Kubernetes cluster – you can enable the last step once you have a `KUBE_CONFIG_DATA` secret.

---

## 4. Adding, Committing, and Pushing

```bash
# 1. Clone the repo (if you haven’t already)
git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome

# 2. Add the new files
git add Dockerfile k8s/deployment.yaml .github/workflows/ci.yml

# 3. Commit
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests, and CI workflow"

# 4. Push to main
git push origin main
```

> **Tip** – If you’re working on a feature branch, create a PR instead of pushing directly to `main`.

---

### Quick sanity check

After pushing, you should see:

* A new **Actions** tab with a successful run.  
* In the **Packages** section of your GitHub repo, the Docker image `ghcr.io/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest` should appear.  
* If you have a Kubernetes cluster configured, the deployment should roll out automatically (or you can apply the manifest manually with `kubectl apply -f k8s/deployment.yaml`).

That’s it! Your Node.js app is now containerised, ready for Kubernetes, and automatically built on every push to `main`. Happy coding!
